prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

You are sitting in Mrs. Caldera’s kitchen, you are sipping a glass of lemonade and trying not to be too curious about the box of plastic hummingbirds behind you, the tray of tineless forks at your elbow. You have heard about the backroom where no one else has ever gone and whatever enters, remains, refrigerator doors, fused coils, mower blades, milk bottles, pistons, gears. “You never know,” she says, rummaging through a cedar chest of recipes, “when something will come of use.” There is a vase of pencil tips on the table, a bowl full of miniature wheels and axles. Upstairs, where her children slept, the doors will not close, the stacks of magazines are burgeoning, there are snow shoes and lampshades, bedsprings and picture tubes, and boxes and boxes of irreducibles! You imagine the headline in the Literalist Express: House Founders Under Weight Of Past. But Mrs Caldera is baking cookies, she is humming a song from childhood, her arms are heavy and strong, they have held babies, a husband, tractor parts and gas tanks, what have they not found a place for? It is getting dark, you have sat for a long time. If you move, you feel something will be disturbed, there is room enough only for your body. “Stay awhile,” Mrs. Caldera says, and never have you felt so valuable.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: You, Mrs, Caldera

outputs.L1:
You are sitting in Mrs. Caldera’s kitchen, sipping a glass of lemonade and trying not to seem too curious about the box of plastic hummingbirds behind you or the tray of tineless forks at your elbow. You have heard about the back room, where no one else has ever gone, and where whatever enters remains: refrigerator doors, fused coils, mower blades, milk bottles, pistons, gears. “You never know,” she says, rummaging through a cedar chest of recipes, “when something will come of use.”

outputs.L2:
You are seated in Mrs. Caldera’s kitchen, drinking lemonade and struggling to keep your curiosity in check about the carton of plastic hummingbirds behind your chair and the tray of prongless forks beside your arm. You have been told about the room in the back, the one no outsider has ever entered, where anything that goes in seems to stay forever: refrigerator doors, melted-together coils, lawn-mower blades, milk bottles, pistons, gears.  

“You never know,” she says, searching through a cedar chest filled with recipes, “when something might turn out to be useful.” On the table sits a vase stuffed with pencil points, along with a bowl containing tiny wheels and axles. Upstairs, in the rooms where her children once slept, the doors can no longer shut; piles of magazines are swelling everywhere, along with snowshoes, lampshades, bed springs, picture tubes, and box after box of things that cannot be reduced any further.  

You picture the headline in the *Literalist Express*: **House Sinks Beneath The Weight Of The Past.**  

But Mrs. Caldera is making cookies and softly singing a tune she has known since childhood. Her arms are solid and powerful; they have carried infants, embraced a husband, lifted tractor parts and gas tanks. What has she ever failed to make room for?  

The day is fading, and you have been sitting there for a long while. You feel that if you so much as shift, something will be upset; there seems to be space for nothing more than your own body.  

“Stay a little longer,” Mrs. Caldera says, and you have never felt more necessary.
outputs.L3:
Mrs. Caldera’s house is crowded with objects she has saved over the years. Everywhere there are things that might seem useless to someone else: plastic hummingbirds, broken forks, machinery parts, and old household items. Instead of throwing them away, she keeps them carefully, believing that any object may one day have a purpose. To her, nothing is completely worthless, because even the most damaged or ordinary item might someday become useful.

Over time, however, this habit of saving has taken over much of the house. The clutter fills rooms and corners, spreading even into the upstairs areas. Some spaces are so packed that the doors no longer close properly. The house feels crowded and difficult to move through, as if the accumulated objects have begun to control the space.

Yet Mrs. Caldera herself does not seem overwhelmed by the disorder. She appears calm, capable, and nurturing. As she bakes cookies and hums, she creates a sense of warmth within the crowded house. Her peaceful behavior contrasts with the chaos around her, suggesting that she finds comfort and meaning in the things she has collected.

For the narrator, the experience is complicated. The crowded rooms make them feel trapped, surrounded by too many objects and too little open space. At the same time, Mrs. Caldera’s kindness changes the feeling of the visit. When she asks the narrator to stay, they feel unexpectedly valued. In a house filled with saved and treasured things, the narrator realizes that they, too, may be seen as someone worth keeping close.
outputs.L4:
You step carefully into Mrs. Caldera’s house because there is no other way to enter it. The front door opens only halfway, stopped by a stack of cardboard boxes softened at the corners and tied with lengths of old ribbon. She smiles as if this is perfectly ordinary, as if every house in the world greets a visitor with resistance before making room. “Mind the lamp,” she says, though the lamp has no shade and no bulb, and is leaning against a chair already occupied by folded newspapers, a chipped blue bowl, three umbrellas, and a shoebox labeled, in her round black handwriting, “buttons, good ones.”

Inside, every surface is claimed. The hallway is lined with towers of magazines, empty jam jars washed clean and shining, biscuit tins full of keys, coils of string, paper bags folded into smaller paper bags, calendars from years that have gone out of use but not, apparently, out of meaning. There are broken radios, cracked plates, wooden spoons worn thin at the bowl, baby shoes with stiff little tongues, a birdcage with no bird in it, a basket of curtain rings, stacks of envelopes slit open neatly along one side, and a chipped porcelain dog whose painted eyes still look loyally toward the door. The house seems less furnished than sedimented, layer upon layer of living deposited in rooms that have learned to hold their breath.

At first you think of the word clutter. It comes to you quickly, almost rudely. You think of fire hazards, dust, narrow paths, of the way the rooms have shrunk around her. You imagine clean white shelves, black garbage bags, decisive hands. But Mrs. Caldera moves through the crowded rooms with such tenderness and precision that your judgment begins to loosen. She does not shove things aside; she addresses them. She lifts a dented kettle from a chair before you sit, apologizing to it as much as to you. She rescues a postcard from the floor and places it on a stack where it seems, somehow, to belong. Nothing in the house is lost to her. Everything has a history, a possible use, a reason it has been spared.

“That jar,” she says, noticing your glance, “is perfect for nails. Not screws. Nails.” She points to another. “That one is for plum jam, if I make any this year.” A length of green velvet may become a cushion cover. A cracked mirror can still brighten a dark corner. A single glove might be needed by someone with one cold hand, and a saucer without a cup can hold lemon seeds, pins, or earrings. Even the useless things are not useless yet. They are waiting for the right need to appear.

The kitchen is the warmest room, though it is hardly a kitchen anymore. Pans hang from hooks beside bunches of dried herbs. The table is covered with oilcloth, letters, a sugar bowl, a basket of receipts, a vase holding pencils instead of flowers, and flowers drying upside down from a pipe. Mrs. Caldera clears a place for you with ceremonial care. She does not sweep the objects away; she relocates them, one by one, as if seating guests at a crowded dinner. Then she pours tea into mismatched cups and sets before you a plate of biscuits from a tin that once held sewing needles, then Christmas cards, then something she cannot remember but refuses to forget.

You begin to understand that her house is not simply full of things. It is full of continuations. Each object extends a person, a day, a gesture, a possibility. A cracked cup remembers the neighbor who brought soup during an illness. A yellow scarf remembers a daughter’s school play. A stack of newspapers contains, somewhere in it, the announcement of a storm, an election, a death, a miracle. Mrs. Caldera does not trust the world’s habit of discarding. She cannot bear the speed with which things are declared finished. In her rooms, nothing is dismissed simply because it is old, damaged, unfashionable, or no longer immediately useful.

And so, strangely, you begin to feel safer there. At first the house seemed to threaten disappearance: objects swallowing space, years swallowing the present. But now it seems to promise the opposite. Here, things are noticed. Here, what has passed through someone’s hands is not thrown away without trial. Here, a life does not have to be clean and efficient in order to matter.

Mrs. Caldera listens to you in the same way she keeps things. When you speak, she does not hurry you toward a point. She allows your sentences their frayed edges and odd detours. She remembers details you barely remember telling her: the name of your childhood dog, the kind of cake you dislike, the fact that you once wanted to learn the accordion. She stores these facts not as gossip but as proof that you have taken shape in her mind. In her presence, you feel labeled in the best sense, placed gently on a shelf where you will not be misplaced.

By the time you leave, the house no longer seems merely overcrowded. It seems devoted. Its abundance is exhausting, inconvenient, perhaps even dangerous, but it is also a form of love: stubborn, excessive, indiscriminate love. Mrs. Caldera’s hoarding is not only an inability to let go. It is a refusal to agree that value belongs only to what is new, whole, or obviously useful. She gives shelter to the broken, the leftover, the almost-forgotten. She believes that everything might still be needed, might still become precious, might still find its moment.

At the door, she presses something into your hand: a small brass button, warm from her palm, engraved with a pattern of leaves. “For your coat,” she says, though your coat has all its buttons. You accept it anyway. Outside, in the clearer air, you look down at the little object and feel an unexpected weight. It is not just a button now. It is evidence that you have been seen, chosen, and added to the vast, tender inventory of Mrs. Caldera’s world.
outputs.L5:
You stood at the edge of the quiet valley, watching the morning mist rise from the ancient caldera. The landscape felt almost unreal, as if the earth itself had once breathed fire and then fallen asleep beneath a blanket of green.

“Beautiful, isn’t it?” asked Mrs. Caldera, her voice gentle but full of pride.

You turned to her and nodded. She knew every stone, every trail, and every story hidden in that place. To most people, it was just an old volcanic crater. To Mrs. Caldera, it was home—a place of memory, mystery, and quiet strength.

As you followed her down the winding path, she pointed to wildflowers growing from the dark soil. “Even after fire,” she said, “life returns.”

And in that moment, you understood why Mrs. Caldera loved the valley so deeply. It was not only a place shaped by the past, but also a reminder that beauty can rise from even the most powerful storms.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short second-person literary vignette about visiting an elderly hoarder’s kitchen, in a whimsical but unsettling tone, with surreal household details and a poignant ending.
counterfactuals.output:
You step into her kitchen sideways, because the door opens only as far as a stack of yellowing newspapers will allow. They are tied with red ribbon, as if each bundle were a present no one has yet deserved.

“Mind the spoons,” she says.

There are spoons everywhere: in jars, in shoes, tucked like silver fish between the pages of cookbooks. One hangs from the ceiling by a length of dental floss, turning slowly though no window is open. The kettle on the stove wears a knitted cap. The sugar bowl has sprouted a fine green moss. From somewhere under the sink comes the delicate ticking of many clocks, none agreeing.

She clears a chair for you by moving three teacups, a cracked globe, and a porcelain goose with human teeth painted along its beak. Her hands tremble, but the tremor seems purposeful, like a small animal trying to escape her sleeves.

“I keep things,” she says, smiling. “Things get lonely.”

You nod, because the room is listening. The cabinets bulge with cans whose labels have faded into weather maps. A loaf of bread on the counter has gone hard and glittering, geode-like, beautiful as a mistake. Above the table, family photographs are clipped to a clothesline: babies, brides, soldiers, a boy with her eyes. Their faces have silvered with age until they look almost underwater.

She makes you tea in a cup patterned with dancing rabbits. When you lift it, a marble rolls out of the saucer and drops to the floor, where it joins a constellation of others beneath the table.

“He used to lose them,” she says softly. “Always underfoot.”

For a moment, the kitchen settles. The spoons stop turning. Even the clocks beneath the sink hold their breath.

Then she reaches across the table and places one small blue marble in your palm, warm from her pocket.

“You can keep this one,” she says.

And because you cannot bear to tell her that some things are gone no matter how carefully they are saved, you close your fingers around it as if it were a tiny world, still whole.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a prose poem in the style of contemporary flash fiction about a woman who saves everything because “you never know when something will come of use.”
counterfactuals.output:
She kept the blue twist ties from bread bags, the silver tongues from soda cans, buttons in a jar that had once held apricot jam. She kept the jam jar too, of course, and the dented lid, and the label she steamed off and flattened in the back of a dictionary under the word *abundance*. 

“You never know when something will come of use,” she said, folding grocery bags into triangles small as secrets.

In her kitchen drawers slept batteries that may or may not have been dead, rubber bands gone pale with age, birthday candles burned down to numbers no one would be again. She saved the string from bakery boxes, the last inch of lipstick, maps of places swallowed by new highways. In the closet: winter coats missing belts, belts missing coats. Under the bed: shoeboxes of photographs with strangers at the edges, their arms half-raised, their mouths beginning to say something the camera interrupted.

People called it clutter. Her daughter called it a fire hazard. The woman called it evidence.

Evidence that things stayed. Evidence that loss could be negotiated with, if you had enough drawers. Evidence that a life, even in fragments, could be made to answer back.

Once, during a storm, the power failed and the whole neighborhood went dark. The woman moved through her rooms by touch, finding candles, matches, a flashlight, a battery that still held one thin vein of light. Later, a boy from next door knocked, shivering, with a torn backpack and rain in his eyelashes. She mended the strap with a needle she had kept in a matchbox, black thread wound around a playing card, and a safety pin from a funeral corsage.

“There,” she said, tugging the seam tight. “Good as.”

He looked at her as if she had performed a miracle.

After he left, she stood in the doorway, watching water run silver down the street. The storm had brought down leaves, branches, someone’s lost receipt, a pink balloon shrunken to a fist. She picked up the balloon and held it gently, as though it might remember floating.

Inside, every shelf leaned toward her. Every box breathed softly in the dark. Nothing was useless yet. Nothing had finished becoming.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical, slightly absurd story set in Mrs. Caldera’s cluttered house, focusing on objects, memory, usefulness, and the feeling of being asked to stay.
counterfactuals.output:
Mrs. Caldera’s house leaned slightly toward the street, as if listening for gossip.

It was not a large house, but it contained the leftovers of several larger lives. Every room had a second room inside it made of objects. In the parlor, towers of newspapers rose like gray reeds from the carpet. In the hallway, umbrellas hung from hooks in a range of broken postures: one black and solemn as a crow, one yellow with only three good ribs, one transparent and freckled with mildew. The dining table had not hosted dinner in twelve years because it was busy holding porcelain birds, half a chess set, six clocks with opinions about different hours, and a glass jar full of buttons that looked like captured moons.

Mrs. Caldera said nothing in the house was useless.

“This spoon,” she told visitors, lifting a bent silver spoon from a teacup full of marbles, “once opened a letter from my sister in Lisbon. This spool of blue thread repaired the hem of a dress I wore the day Mr. Caldera asked me to dance. This chipped vase frightens ants. This paper bag remembers peaches.”

The visitors usually nodded in the careful way people nod when they are looking for a place to put their hands.

But the objects knew she was right.

At night, when Mrs. Caldera slept in her narrow bed between a stack of hatboxes and a lamp without a shade, the house loosened its breath. The clocks cleared their throats. The spoons shifted in drawers. The porcelain birds rehearsed the names of extinct winds. The paper bag on the shelf above the stove whispered, “Peaches, peaches,” until the kitchen smelled faintly of summer and bruise.

There was a blue armchair in the sitting room, collapsed on one side and patched with two squares of green fabric. It had been asked many times if it wished to be taken away.

“Never,” said the armchair, though no one had asked aloud. “Here I am useful. Here I hold the shape of her waiting.”

And it was true: Mrs. Caldera sat in it every afternoon at four, when the light entered the window like a polite animal and lay across her knees. She would drink tea, though sometimes the tea was only hot water that had once stood near a lemon. She would speak to Mr. Caldera, whose photograph lived on the mantel between a seashell and a ceramic frog.

“You see how the world behaves,” she would say. “It keeps trying to leave.”

In the photograph, Mr. Caldera wore a hat too small for his head and an expression of mild astonishment, as if he had just learned that clouds were not furniture.

One October morning, a young man from the council came to the house with a clipboard and a smile trained to be gentle at the edges. His name was Paul. He stood on the porch while vines touched his sleeve and the doorbell hummed a long uncertain note.

Mrs. Caldera opened the door carrying a colander full of keys.

“Are you here for the piano?” she asked.

“No, ma’am,” said Paul. “I’m here about the complaint.”

“The piano has complained?”

“The neighbors, ma’am.”

“Ah,” she said. “They do enjoy it.”

Paul glanced past her into the hallway, where a mountain of coats leaned against the wall as though frozen in the act of departing. He smelled dust, lavender, old paper, and something like soup remembering itself.

“There are concerns,” he said, “about safety. About accumulation.”

Mrs. Caldera looked down at the colander. The keys glittered faintly, though most belonged to doors no longer standing.

“Accumulation,” she repeated. “That is a word invented by people who do not love anything in particular.”

Paul was young enough to believe in surfaces and old enough to be tired. His own apartment had three plates, one plant, and a mattress that had never heard a lullaby. He had been told that a useful object was an object currently performing its assigned function. A chair was useful if sat upon. A cup was useful if filled. A life was useful if it moved efficiently between appointments.

Inside Mrs. Caldera’s house, this definition began to sweat.

“May I come in?” he asked.

“Only if you are not allergic to violins.”

“I don’t think so.”

“No one does at first.”

She let him in.

The house received him with a thousand small stares: drawer handles, brass knobs, painted eyes, the dark lenses of three broken cameras. Paul stepped around a basket of pinecones, a stack of atlases, and a toy horse with no legs but tremendous dignity.

“What is all this?” he asked, unable to stop himself.

Mrs. Caldera beamed. “Evidence.”

“Of what?”

“That time passed through here and took off its shoes.”

They moved slowly from room to room. Mrs. Caldera introduced things as if hosting a party.

“This is the umbrella I carried when the doctor said my son would live. This is the pan that burned the first meal I cooked as a wife. This is a drawer of instructions for machines I no longer own, because one must not abandon the idea of repair. This is a bowl of foreign coins. This is a hat for a child who became a dentist. This is a ribbon from a cake box, but the cake itself was terrible, so the ribbon has had to remember the occasion alone.”

Paul wrote nothing on his clipboard.

In the kitchen, a ladder stood in the corner wearing a scarf. A radio sat on the counter, silent and plugged into nothing. There were jars of screws, jars of nails, jars of seeds, jars of beads, jars of things too small or too mysterious to declare themselves. On the windowsill, three dead flies lay arranged like punctuation.

“You can’t keep everything,” Paul said softly.

Mrs. Caldera turned toward him. Her face was lined not like paper crumpled, but like a map folded many times to find the same beloved place.

“Who told you that?”

“No one. It’s just—there isn’t room.”

“For what?”

“For living.”

At this, the house became very quiet. Even the clocks hesitated.

Mrs. Caldera placed the colander of keys on the stove.

“My dear,” she said, “this is how I do it.”

Paul looked at the towers of tins and rags and jars, at the chair keeping its old promise, at the paper bag full of peaches that were no longer there. He thought of his apartment, its clean white walls, the single cup drying upside down beside the sink. Nothing in his rooms asked him where he had been. Nothing accused him of forgetting. Nothing needed him to stay.

A teaspoon slid from the counter and landed at his feet.

He bent to pick it up. It was tarnished, its bowl warped into a small silver moon.

“That one,” said Mrs. Caldera, “stirred cough syrup into ginger tea the winter I could not stop shaking.”

Paul held it carefully. It was heavier than he expected.

Outside, the wind pressed its face against the windows. The house creaked, not ominously, but conversationally. Somewhere upstairs, a trunk settled deeper into its own memory.

“I’m supposed to make a report,” Paul said.

“Of course,” said Mrs. Caldera. “Make it useful.”

He nearly laughed. Instead he followed her into the back room, which she called the conservatory, though nothing grew there except dust and a stubborn geranium in a cracked mug. The room was almost impassable. Boxes filled the floor. Lamps without bulbs tilted in every corner. A bicycle wheel hung from the ceiling by a red cord, slowly turning though there was no breeze.

In the center of the room stood a small wooden stool.

It was plain, three-legged, nicked along the edges. Compared to the rest of the household, it seemed almost naked.

“What’s that?” Paul asked.

Mrs. Caldera looked at it for a long time.

“That,” she said, “is something I don’t remember.”

The words fell strangely. Around them, the objects rustled in distress.

“I find that rude of me,” she continued. “It has stayed all these years, and I cannot recall why I asked it to.”

Paul crouched beside the stool. It had a faint stain on the seat shaped like a continent. One leg had been repaired with twine.

“Maybe it was just a stool,” he said.

Mrs. Caldera frowned. “Nothing is just.”

The stool said nothing. If it had a memory, it kept it folded tight.

Paul imagined it in another life: holding a pail, a foot, a child reaching for jam, a man changing a lightbulb, a woman resting between chores. Perhaps usefulness did not always leave a dramatic mark. Perhaps some things served by being beneath us when we did not notice we needed height. Perhaps the stool had been faithful in the ordinary way, which is the easiest to overlook and the hardest to replace.

“I think,” Paul said slowly, “it helped someone reach something.”

Mrs. Caldera’s eyes sharpened.

“Yes?”

“Maybe something high.”

“All the important things are either too high or under the bed.”

“Maybe a jar.”

“No.”

“A book?”

“No.”

“A star?”

She smiled. “Closer.”

Then she put one hand on the wall, as though steadying not herself but the room. “My son,” she said. “He stood on it to look through the little window in the pantry. He said the moon followed him from room to room. He wanted to catch it in a bowl.”

The stool seemed to grow brighter, though it was only afternoon light shifting through the grimy panes.

“There,” Mrs. Caldera whispered. “There you are.”

Paul touched the stool’s edge. For a moment, absurdly, he felt thanked.

When they returned to the parlor, the blue armchair waited with its permanent sag. Mrs. Caldera lowered herself into it. The chair accepted her with a sigh so tender Paul had to look away.

“Do you have many things?” she asked him.

“No.”

“Ah. You must be very lonely.”

He wanted to object. Instead he thought of his three plates stacked like obedient thoughts, his plant browning at the tips, his bed that forgot him each morning.

“I’m busy,” he said.

“Busy is a way of being lonely while moving.”

One of the clocks struck seven, though it was barely five. Another answered with eleven. A third made a noise like a spoon dropped into a well.

Paul stood with his clipboard against his chest. The official words waited inside it: hazard, obstruction, removal, compliance. They were clean words, broom words, words with gloves on.

But the house was looking at him.

Not pleading. Not exactly.

Asking.

Stay, said the umbrellas with their broken ribs. Stay, said the jars of screws, each screw still dreaming of wood. Stay, said the photograph of Mr. Caldera, astonished forever. Stay, said the stool, newly remembered. Stay, said the paper bag, peaches, peaches. Stay, said the blue chair, because holding someone is honest work.

Paul understood then that Mrs. Caldera’s house was not cluttered because she could not let go.

It was cluttered because so many things had asked not to be vanished, and she, unlike most people, had answered.

He removed a pen from his pocket.

“What are you writing?” she asked.

“A report.”

“Am I condemned?”

“Not today.”

“What am I?”

Paul looked around. At the avalanche of ordinary relics. At the mess of memory refusing to become trash. At the dangerous, tender architecture of being needed.

“Occupied,” he said.

Mrs. Caldera laughed. The house laughed with her: teacups chimed, floorboards clapped, newspapers shivered in their gray skins. Even the silent radio gave one brief burst of static, like applause from another century.

Before he left, Mrs. Caldera pressed something into his hand.

It was a button, brown, chipped, unremarkable.

“What is it for?” he asked.

“You’ll find out,” she said.

Paul walked home in the early dark with the button warm in his palm. The moon followed him from street to street, ridiculous and persistent, like a face at every window. When he reached his apartment, he noticed how bare it was, how the air had nothing to trip over, how the silence had been swept clean.

He placed the button on the windowsill.

It did not match anything. It did not fix anything. It did not perform.

Still, the room changed around it.

The button sat there, small as a period at the end of a sentence that had finally asked him to remain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, imaginative paragraph narrated in second person about sitting in a kitchen full of strange collected junk, blending humor, melancholy, and tenderness.
counterfactuals.output: You sit at the kitchen table among the holy inventory of your ridiculous life: a cracked blue teapot wearing a knitted hat, three keys to houses that have forgotten you, a jar of buttons labeled EMERGENCY EYES, the porcelain cow creamer your aunt stole from a diner in 1978, dead batteries in a teacup, postcards from cities that look happier than they were, a whisk bent like a question mark, and the small green radio that only catches weather reports and one preacher with a voice like frying onions. The room smells of old toast, dust, and basil trying nobly to outlive the windowsill; the refrigerator hums with the patient despair of a monk. You laugh because the pepper grinder is shaped like the Eiffel Tower and has outlasted two loves, one dog, and your faith in ergonomic design. Still, when the evening leans its gray forehead against the glass, you touch the chipped mug beside you as if it were a hand. All this junk, you think, has been quietly practicing devotion: holding, surviving, waiting to be useful again.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short literary scene where an old woman baking cookies has filled her home with salvaged parts, obsolete objects, and “irreducibles,” ending with the visitor feeling unexpectedly valuable.
counterfactuals.output:
The old woman’s kitchen smelled of molasses, orange peel, and warm dust. While the cookies browned, she moved through the house with the slow authority of someone tending a museum after hours.

Everywhere, things waited.

A brass doorknob without a door. Clock hands in a saucer. The glass eye of a dismantled lamp. Drawers full of keys labeled in her tiny script: *opens nothing now*, *possibly suitcase*, *from Martin’s blue coat*. Along the windowsill sat a row of obsolete objects—film canisters, fountain-pen nibs, a rotary phone with its finger holes polished by vanished callers.

“And these?” I asked, touching a shelf of small, nameless bits: a bent hinge, a chipped porcelain knob, a triangle of blue tile, a screw with no thread left.

“My irreducibles,” she said, sliding a tray from the oven. “Things that have become only themselves.”

The cookies emerged cracked and golden, each one holding a dark thumbprint of jam. She set them on a cooling rack beside a radio that no longer received anything but weather and static.

“I keep parts,” she said, “because the world is always throwing away what it doesn’t immediately understand.”

I laughed softly, though I had spent the whole visit feeling too large for the narrow rooms, too modern, too unemployed, too recently left by someone who had found me inconvenient.

The old woman placed a cookie in my hand. It was warm, almost alive.

“You, for instance,” she said, as if continuing a thought. “You may not know what you fit yet. That doesn’t mean you’re spare.”

Outside, the evening gathered itself in the gutters. Inside, among the salvaged hinges, dead clocks, and faithful useless keys, I stood holding the cookie carefully, as though I too had been rescued from a box at the curb and brought into light.
